outline.chapter_title: Case Background, Facts, and Procedural Posture
outline.description: Introduces the parties, the disputed overtime pay policy, the claims and remedies sought under Minnesota wage statutes, the employer’s post-suit payments, the parties’ stipulations, and the summary judgment and appellate standards governing review.
subtopics: Parties and roles: Bruce Cohen (hourly licensed attorney reviewer) and Consilio, LLC (legal document review company with Minnesota offices)
2019 policy change: email announcement eliminating overtime premium pay; paying all hours at base rate beginning August 2019
Claims filed in August 2020: MPWA (§§ 181.101, 181.171), MFLSA (§§ 177.25, 177.27), MWTA (§ 181.032) seeking overtime, liquidated damages, penalties, and injunctive relief
Consilio’s post-suit payments: $256,010.01 to Minnesota reviewers to cover MFLSA overtime and liquidated damages; Cohen received $3,225.21 (overtime) and $462 (liquidated damages)
Key stipulations: Cohen has been paid all overtime wages and MFLSA liquidated damages alleged; dispute narrowed to statutory penalties and injunctive relief
Summary judgment posture: parties agreed to have court decide statutory claims before further discovery; district court granted summary judgment to Consilio on all claims
Appellate standard: de novo review of summary judgment; no genuine dispute of material fact and entitlement to judgment as a matter of law; evidence viewed in light most favorable to Cohen

outline.chapter_title: MPWA Claim: Who Can Obtain Average Daily Wage Penalties
outline.description: Analyzes whether an employee suing under the MPWA may recover average daily wage penalties for late or unpaid wages, focusing on the text and structure of §§ 181.101 and 181.171 and Minnesota interpretive canons.
subtopics: Statutory framework: § 181.171 (private civil action for violations and recovery of compensatory damages and penalties if provided in the violated section); § 181.101(a) (timely payment of wages; Commissioner’s enforcement powers)
Textual focus: § 181.101 references only the Commissioner’s ability to demand, charge, and collect wages and penalties; employee retains right to prosecute a claim for wages (not penalties)

Comparative statutory design: Minnesota Legislature expressly authorizes employee penalties in §§ 181.13 and 181.14 (discharge/quit contexts), showing it ‘knows how’ to grant employees penalty rights when intended

Canons and cases: plain meaning rule (Allan v. R.D. Offutt); money collected by Commissioner paid to employee (Milner v. Farmers Ins. Exch.); district court readings (Hull v. ConvergeOne) limiting penalty enforcement to Commissioner under § 181.101

Holding on MPWA: Only the Commissioner may seek average daily wage penalties under § 181.101; employees may sue for wages but not penalties; affirmance of summary judgment for Consilio on MPWA penalties

outline.chapter_title: MFLSA Claim: Statutory Penalties, Article III, and Mootness
outline.description: Explains the court’s decision to vacate and remand the MFLSA claim for a jurisdictional determination, addressing the interplay among statutory penalties payable to the state, standing, voluntary cessation, and mootness.
subtopics: Scope of remaining dispute: Cohen stipulated he received all MFLSA overtime and liquidated damages; only statutory penalties remain at issue
Penalty payee: parties agree MFLSA statutory penalties are payable to the Commissioner, not to Cohen personally
Article III requirements: standing must exist for each claim and remedy and must persist throughout litigation (Town of Chester; Sisney on mootness continuity)

Deterrent effect and civil penalties: Laidlaw recognizes penalties can redress ongoing or threatened harm by deterring violations; but claims may become moot if it is absolutely clear the conduct will not recur
Factual uncertainty: record does not resolve whether Consilio’s allegedly unlawful overtime policy remains in place; this fact determines mootness and thus jurisdiction

Disposition: Vacatur of summary judgment on MFLSA claim and remand for the district court to determine jurisdiction (standing/mootness) in light of whether the policy persists or has been discontinued with no reasonable expectation of recurrence

Concurring perspective: questions whether Laidlaw’s rationale for penalties supports standing under MFLSA and notes differences in penalty schemes; suggests district court may address mootness first on remand

outline.chapter_title: MWTA Notice Claim and Injunctive Relief: Preservation and Waiver
outline.description: Covers the court’s affirmance on the MWTA and injunctive relief issues, emphasizing the lack of statutory authority for employee penalties under the MWTA claim as argued and the failure to properly preserve a new form of injunctive relief.
subtopics: MWTA theory: alleged failure to provide required notice of pay policy change (§ 181.032(d)(4), (f))
Relief mismatch: Cohen stipulated he was paid all amounts owed and identified no statutory basis for civil penalties under the MWTA provisions invoked
Appellate waiver: lack of developed argument or legal authority to reverse; application of waiver doctrine (Milligan v. City of Red Oak); affirmance of dismissal
Injunctive relief evolution: complaint sought specific injunctions; later summary judgment briefing requested a different injunction (rescinding 2019 policy)

Procedural bar: new claims or materially different relief must be sought via amended complaint (Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)); courts will not consider new theories raised only in briefing (InfoDeli, LLC); affirmance on injunctive relief

outline.description: Synthesizes the holdings and their implications for pleading, proof, and remedies in Minnesota wage cases, and highlights strategic and compliance takeaways.
subtopics: Disposition: Affirmed on MPWA, MWTA, and injunctive relief; vacated and remanded on MFLSA penalties for jurisdictional determination
Remedial architecture matters: under § 181.101 MPWA penalties are enforceable only by the Commissioner; employees may pursue unpaid wages in court but not Commissioner penalties
Article III vigilance: where only government-payable penalties remain, plaintiffs must show ongoing or reasonably expected future violations to avoid mootness
Stipulations narrow cases: agreeing that wages and liquidated damages are fully paid can convert a case into a pure-penalty dispute, raising jurisdictional risks
Preservation and pleading discipline: seek desired injunctive relief in the complaint or via amendment; avoid raising new remedies in summary judgment briefing

Employer compliance note: changes to overtime policies implicate multiple Minnesota statutes; properly notice changes (MWTA), ensure timely payment (MPWA), and maintain compliant pay practices to avoid MFLSA exposure
